title: Elastic micro-reservations and isolation attenuation PRD
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Summary: This PRD proposes 'Elastic Micro-Reservations' (EMR) — a new lightweight reservation primitive for Redwood Dedicated that lets customers allocate small, time-windowed slices of capacity with configurable headroom and automated backfill. Paired with a new 'isolation attenuation' policy, EMR reduces noisy-neighbor disruption by softly shrinking non-reserved headroom before hard preemption. Goals: 1) Give mid-size tenants a predictable low-latency allocation without requiring large reserved pools. 2) Reduce hard preemptions and SLA violations during transient spikes. 3) Provide clear telemetry and controls in the Redwood Console so customers can tune micro-reserves and view reconciliation metrics. Background: Existing reserved pools are coarse-grained and require significant commitment. Many customers ask for predictable short-lived capacity (e.g., warm-up for scale events, feature launches) but cannot commit to monthly reserved capacity. Engineering telemetry and customer incident traces show a class of spikes (~10-60s) where the platform either preempts aggressively or yields unpredictable latency for reserved tenants. EMR is designed to bridge the gap between ad hoc burst and reserved pools by offering small, elastic guarantees with automated decay and explicit reconciliation.
requirements: API: POST /v1/dedicated/reservations to create an EMR with fields: tenant_id, min_tokens_per_sec, max_tokens_per_sec, window_seconds, burst_credits, policy: {fallback: prefer-cache|fallback-model|defer}, name

Server: scheduler support for per-tenant micro-reservations with sliding-window credit accounting and time-decay. Credits should be consumable at token-level granularity and support fractional refill rates.
Runtime: isolation attenuation algorithm that reduces non-reserved headroom proportionally over a configurable attenuation window before any hard eviction occurs.

Console: new UI panel under Dedicated > Reservations showing active EMRs, current credit balance, historical reconciliation (consumed vs allocated), and shorthand tuning presets (Launch, Sustained, Spike).

Telemetry: metrics emitted per reservation: reservation_id, tenant_id, allocated_rps_min, allocated_rps_max, consumed_tokens, overage_events, attenuation_events, preemption_events. Dashboards to show reconciliation across zones and per-tenant latency SLO impact.
RBAC/Audit: creation/update/deletion are logged in audit trail with who/when and include reservation parameters. KMS metadata tagging for Private customers where required.
Fallbacks: define fallback model variants and region routing for when an EMR cannot be satisfied; platform must expose decision reason codes in API responses and console logs.

SLA: when EMR is active, reserved min_rps must meet 95th percentile token latency target (configurable; default 200ms) for the tenant's requests served on dedicated capacity unless downstream failures occur.
Operational: ability to forcibly revoke or scale a reservation from the console and a read-only /v1/dedicated/reservations/{id} API for inspection.
Limits: default per-organization cap of 20 concurrent EMRs; quota increases by support request.
non_goals: Not a replacement for long-term reserved pools or enterprise monthly capacity contracts.
Not supporting cross-tenant pooling or shared reservations in this phase.
No changes to billing model in initial rollout; usage will be billed via existing per-token billing and a visible reservation telemetry tag for post-hoc invoicing analysis.
No on-prem agent changes in initial MVP (Private customers get API and console metadata only).
tradeoffs_and_decisions: Design chose proportional attenuation (gradual reduction) over binary eviction to reduce tail latency spikes for reserved tenants at the cost of slightly higher complexity in scheduler accounting.
Credits are token-granular rather than request-granular to better align with Redwood's per-token billing and to enable partial consumption for streaming responses.
Initial cap of 20 EMRs/org minimizes resource fragmentation risk; this can be increased after telemetry review.
We defer billing productization (add-on fee, committed credits) to a later phase to speed launch and collect usage patterns.
Fallbacks: prefer-cache fallback prioritized to reduce model-switch regressions where possible; where cache not applicable, we route to a lower-cost variant before failing requests.
Console first: we prioritize operational visibility (console + metrics) before complex developer SDK bindings to limit UX surface at launch.
acceptance_criteria: Create EMR via API: can create, retrieve, update (min/max/window/name), and delete a reservation. API returns reservation_id and current_credit_balance.
Scheduler honors min_rps: under normal load, a tenant with an active EMR receives at least the configured min_rps for 95% of 1-minute windows in a controlled canary test.

Attenuation behavior validated: when node pressure increases, non-reserved headroom is reduced incrementally over configured attenuation window; tests show fewer than 10% hard preemptions across simulated noisy neighbors compared to baseline.
Telemetry completeness: dashboards show reservation consumption, attenuation events, overage events and reconciliation within 5 minutes of occurrence.
Console UX delivered: Reservations panel implements list/detail flow, create wizard with three tuning presets, and an action to revoke immediately; UI tests pass.
Fallback codes surfaced: API responses include decision_reason and fallback_variant where applicable; unit/integration tests assert presence.
Audit logs: every create/update/delete writes an audit entry with user, timestamp, and parameter snapshot for both hosted and Dedicated customers.
Security review: security_review_required = "true" and security team signoff recorded in dependencies before release to Private customers.
Load test: scaled canary with 50 tenants, 10% with EMRs, shows no SLO regressions for existing reserved-pool customers and median tail-latency within 10% of baseline.
rollout_plan: Phase 0 - Internal canary (2 weeks): implement scheduler + API + minimal console; enable EMR for internal tenants in us-east-1 only.
Phase 1 - Public canary (4 weeks): opt-in for customers via feature flag; collect telemetry, adjust attenuation curves and limits.
Phase 2 - General availability (6+ weeks after Phase 1): console GA, default limits, docs, and integration tests; announce to sales and add support playbook.

Rollback criteria: sustained >5% increase in P95 token latency for reserved-pool customers for 15 minutes, or >0.5% increase in errors attributable to scheduler failures; safety rollback toggles available to SRE.
Support & runbook: include oncall playbook, escalation path, and a reconciliation dashboard for Finance to map consumed tokens to reservation IDs.
